nameStory: The pustulated carrion beetle gets its name from the small bumps or blisters (pustules) that dot its body surface, giving it a distinctive textured appearance. The word 'pustulated' comes from the Latin 'pustula' meaning a small swelling or blister, which perfectly describes this beetle's bumpy exterior. Like other carrion beetles, it's named for its association with dead animals, though this species has some surprising twists on that lifestyle!
description: The pustulated carrion beetle is a robust, black beetle about half an inch long with distinctive orange-red markings on its wing covers. What makes it instantly recognizable are the small, raised bumps scattered across its body that look like tiny blisters or pustules. Unlike most of its burying beetle relatives that work with dead animals, this species has evolved some unusual behaviors. It belongs to a group of beetles known for their remarkable parental care and cooperative breeding behaviors.

idTips.label: Pustulated surface
idTips.description: The body is covered with small, raised bumps that feel rough to the touch, like tiny blisters scattered across the beetle's surface - this is the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Orange-red markings
idTips.description: Bright orange to reddish patches on the black wing covers create a striking contrast, often in irregular bands or spots

idTips.label: Clubbed antennae
idTips.description: The antennae end in distinctive club-like structures that are orange in color and help the beetle detect chemical signals

idTips.label: Robust build
idTips.description: About half an inch long with a sturdy, somewhat flattened body built for digging and moving through soil and leaf litter

idTips.label: Exposed wing tips
idTips.description: The shortened wing covers leave the tip of the abdomen visible, typical of the burying beetle group

habitat: Look for pustulated carrion beetles in mixed woodlands, forest edges, and areas with rich organic soil throughout New England's lower elevations. They're often found in habitats where small mammals like shrews and voles are common, as they have a unique relationship with these creatures. Unlike other carrion beetles that prefer open areas near carcasses, this species tends to stay closer to dense vegetation and underground burrows.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and become active as soil warms, beginning their unusual breeding behaviors. This is when you're most likely to spot them moving through leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible and engaged in their remarkable parenting behaviors. Look for them in early morning or evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Adults may still be active in early fall, preparing for overwintering. New adults from summer breeding may appear before temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter underground in soil or deep leaf litter, remaining inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: This beetle may be the only known insect that acts as a true parasitoid of living vertebrates - instead of just eating dead animals like its relatives, it has been observed parasitizing live shrews and other small mammals, making it one of nature's most unusual predator-prey relationships!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other burying beetles, but the pustulated surface texture is unique - run your finger gently over the beetle and you'll feel the distinctive bumpy texture that no other New England burying beetle has. Remember: 'pustules = pustulated' for an easy memory trick.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'carrion beetle,' this species breaks the family rules by potentially parasitizing living animals rather than just recycling dead ones. This makes it somewhat of a black sheep in the burying beetle world, showing how evolution can take surprising turns even within closely related species.
compareHints: Unlike the smooth-bodied tomentose burying beetle or the roundneck sexton beetle, the pustulated carrion beetle's bumpy texture is unmistakable. While other burying beetles in New England have orange markings, none have the distinctive pustulated surface. The habitat preferences also differ - while most burying beetles seek out large carcasses in open areas, this species stays closer to small mammal territories in denser vegetation.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the Roundneck Sexton Beetle which has a distinctly rounded pronotum (the shield behind the head) and more irregular orange markings, the Tomentose Burying Beetle has more angular, rectangular orange patches and a less pronounced 'neck' region.
Among its Nicrophorus relatives, the Roundneck Sexton Beetle stands out with its neat, rectangular orange patches and notably rounded pronotum.
Say's Burying Beetle differs from the Tomentose Burying Beetle by having less fuzzy body hair and different orange marking patterns.
